card.tagline: A ballet dance for four performers showing virtuosity and symmetry.
card.profile: Pas de quatre, literally 'step of four' in French, is a ballet dance executed by four performers. Developed in the nineteenth century, it frequently repeats the classical construction of the pas de deux expanded for four dancers, featuring an entrée, individual variations, and a coda. Most pas de quatre are non-narrative divertissements designed to exhibit pure classical technique and artistry, though narrative and standalone versions also exist. Historical landmarks range from Jules Perrot's 1845 showcase to Lev Ivanov's 1895 Danse des petits cygnes in Swan Lake.
card.insight: In London in 1845, Jules Perrot gathered four rival ballerinas for a pas de quatre that Queen Victoria attended.

card.profile_long:
Pas de quatre is a French ballet term meaning literally 'step of four', identifying a classical choreography performed by four dancers. During the nineteenth century, the structure of the pas de quatre developed into a formal suite mirroring the architecture of the classical pas de deux, comprising an opening entrée, solo variations for the dancers, and an energetic concluding coda. Although primarily conceived as plotless divertissements that function as dazzling exhibitions of academic technique and musical artistry within larger stage works, choreographers have also created standalone pas de quatre and expressive, narrative quartets across the history of the art form.

The most famous early milestone arrived in 1845 at Her Majesty's Theatre in London. Choreographer Jules Perrot set a standalone Pas de Quatre to music composed by Cesare Pugni, uniting four of the most celebrated ballerinas of the Romantic era: Lucile Grahn, Carlotta Grisi, Fanny Cerrito, and Marie Taglioni. While Fanny Elssler had declined the invitation to participate, the young Lucile Grahn accepted without hesitation. The production became an instant sensation; at the third performance, Queen Victoria and Prince Albert were in attendance, though personal friction and professional rivalries among the four star ballerinas limited the engagement to only four performances.

In 1895, Lev Ivanov created one of the most recognizable pas de quatre in history for Act 2 of Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, titled Danse des petits cygnes. Performed by four dancers—typically demi-soloists chosen from the corps de ballet—the piece requires dancers to cross and link their hands throughout, executing immaculate, synchronized, and rapid footwork across the stage. A few years later, in 1898, Marius Petipa choreographed an ebullient all-male quartet in Act 3 of Alexander Glazunov's Raymonda, titled Variation pour quatre danseurs within the Pas classique hongrois, originally staged for Sergei Legat, Georgi Kyasht, Nikolai Legat, and Alexander Gorsky.

During the twentieth century, choreographers adapted the format beyond purely classical divertissements to explore drama, modern movement, and neoclassical abstraction. In 1936, Antony Tudor presented Jardin aux Lilas to music by Ernest Chausson, featuring four principal characters supported by a corps de ballet. In 1949, modern dance pioneer José Limón choreographed The Moor's Pavane to music by Henry Purcell, basing the four-dancer interaction on Shakespeare's tragedy Othello. Neoclassical master George Balanchine expanded the concept mathematically in his 1957 work Agon to music by Igor Stravinsky, incorporating a pas de quatre for four men, a double pas de quatre for eight women, and a triple pas de quatre for twelve dancers. In 1975, Kenneth MacMillan choreographed 'Spring' in The Four Seasons to Giuseppe Verdi's music, showing that the quartet format continues to serve diverse aesthetic styles across the theatrical canon.

sections.origins_and_history: Pas de quatre originated in the classical ballet tradition as a dance for four performers. During the nineteenth century, its classical structure solidified around an entrée, solo variations, and a coda. Jules Perrot established the benchmark in 1845 with his London work for four leading Romantic ballerinas, and Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov further cemented the format in late-nineteenth-century Russian classical repertory.
sections.how_it_is_danced: In standard classical structure, the pas de quatre begins with an entrée, transitions into individual variations for each dancer, and finishes with a shared coda. In Lev Ivanov's 1895 Danse des petits cygnes, the four dancers perform with cross-linked hands, executing precise and dazzling footwork in strict synchronization. Combinations can be all-female, all-male, or mixed ensembles.
sections.music_and_instruments: Major compositions associated with the format include Cesare Pugni's 1845 score for Perrot, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's music for Swan Lake (1895), Alexander Glazunov's score for Raymonda (1898), Ernest Chausson's music for Jardin aux Lilas (1936), Henry Purcell's music for The Moor's Pavane (1949), Igor Stravinsky's score for Agon (1957), and Giuseppe Verdi's music for Kenneth MacMillan's The Four Seasons (1975).
sections.costume_and_setting: The setting depends on the theatrical context, ranging from nineteenth-century opera houses such as Her Majesty's Theatre in London to classical and modern stages worldwide. In Danse des petits cygnes, performers appear as cygnets in the lakeside setting of Swan Lake Act 2.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Pas de quatre are usually plotless dances performed as divertissements to display technique and artistry within larger ballets. However, narrative works also exist, such as José Limón's The Moor's Pavane, which interprets Shakespeare's Othello, and Antony Tudor's Jardin aux Lilas, which explores emotional entanglements.
sections.notable_figures: Key choreographers include Jules Perrot, Lev Ivanov, Marius Petipa, Antony Tudor, José Limón, George Balanchine, and Kenneth MacMillan. Notable original performers include Marie Taglioni, Carlotta Grisi, Fanny Cerrito, Lucile Grahn, Sergei Legat, Georgi Kyasht, Nikolai Legat, Alexander Gorsky, Maude Lloyd, Hugh Laing, Peggy van Praagh, Betty Jones, Lucas Hoving, Pauline Koner, Lesley Collier, Michael Coleman, David Ashmole, and Wayne Eagling.
sections.regional_variants: The pas de quatre has appeared across European, Russian, and American ballet traditions, with adaptations ranging from the French classical divertissement and British dramatic ballet to American neoclassical works and modern dance pavanes. A ballroom dance sharing the name pas de quatre also existed.
sections.lineage: The pas de quatre developed directly from the structure of the classical pas de deux, expanding the architecture of entrée, variations, and coda to accommodate four dancers.

teaching.formation: Four dancers performing together, often in line with cross-linked hands as seen in Danse des petits cygnes, or alternating in entrée, solo variations, and coda.
teaching.level_notes: Demi-soloists or principal dancers execute precise footwork and variations.

claims.text: Pas de quatre is a French term meaning 'step of four', identifying a ballet dance for four people.
They are usually plotless dances performed as divertissements, though narrative versions also exist.
In the nineteenth century, the pas de quatre developed a structure comprising an entrée, variations, and coda.
Jules Perrot's 1845 Pas de Quatre was danced by Lucile Grahn, Carlotta Grisi, Fanny Cerrito, and Marie Taglioni.
Only four performances of Perrot's ballet were given due to personal difficulties among the star dancers, with Queen Victoria and Prince Albert attending the third.
In the 1895 Swan Lake Danse des petits cygnes, four dancers with cross-linked hands perform precise, dazzling footwork.
Raymonda in 1898 included a variation for four male dancers choreographed by Marius Petipa to music by Alexander Glazunov.
José Limón based his 1949 work The Moor's Pavane on Shakespeare's Othello for a cast of four dancers.

music_profile.sound_description: The music spans Romantic, late-nineteenth-century Russian imperial, and twentieth-century neoclassical orchestral styles. Built around formal sections including an opening entrée, character variations, and an accelerating coda, the music provides clear metric support for athletic displays, lyricism, and synchronized footwork.

movement_profile.footwork: Precise and dazzling footwork, as exemplified by the petit allegro in Danse des petits cygnes.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Cross-linked hands among four performers in line, or classical port de bras.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Quartet formation, line of four with linked hands, or alternating solo and ensemble staging.
movement_profile.partnering: Group ensemble work of four dancers, either with cross-linked hands or structured solo entrances.

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Lack of musical synchronization among the four performers; breaking hand holds during linked formations.

episode_brief.title_hook: Four Ballerinas and a Royal Audience
episode_brief.logline: How four of Europe's greatest 19th-century ballet stars were united on one London stage, forging the legendary pas de quatre.
beats: London, 1845: Jules Perrot brings four rival prima ballerinas together at Her Majesty's Theatre.
The delicate diplomacy of casting: Fanny Elssler declines, Lucile Grahn accepts, joining Grisi, Cerrito, and Taglioni.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert attend the third performance of Perrot's four-show run.
St. Petersburg, 1895: Lev Ivanov invents the linked-arms line in Swan Lake's Danse des petits cygnes.
The twentieth-century evolution: Tudor, Limón, and Balanchine transform the four-dancer form into psychological drama and modern neoclassicism.

lesson_ladder.goal: Recreate the cross-linked hands hold used in Danse des petits cygnes.
drills: Form a four-person line and practice alternating forearm crosses.
Step in unison across the floor without pulling on neighboring hands.
Match musical counts across all four performers.

lesson_ladder.goal: Structure the flow between group entrance, solo sections, and final coda.
drills: Practice clearing the stage for individual variation solos.
Re-enter in unison for the rapid coda finish.

visual_motifs: Four pairs of pointe shoes moving in absolute unison.
Cross-linked hands creating an unbroken chain across the stage.
Nineteenth-century theatrical playbills and lithographs of Romantic ballerinas.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An exacting ballet maître or répétiteur focused on spatial symmetry, impeccable timing, and historical styling.
episode_brief.music_cue: The crisp, rhythmic woodwinds and strings of Cesare Pugni's 1845 Pas de Quatre or Tchaikovsky's Danse des petits cygnes.

evidence.observation: Dancers performing ballet turns and jumps across the floor in pointe shoes

observation.setting: Dance studio with white walls, mirrors, ballet barres along the sides, and a wooden or sprung floor, during a rehearsal with an instructor present.
observation.dancers: Four female ballet dancers in practice clothes, plus other dancers practicing in the background.
observation.formation_and_space: In a horizontal line facing sideways/front, holding hands in a linked chain across their bodies.
observation.posture: Upright classical ballet posture, straight spine, turned-out legs, weight centered over pointe shoes.
observation.footwork: Pointe work involving rapid low jumps, bourrées, quick weight shifts, and extensions (battements) timed to the musical beats.
observation.arms_and_hands: Arms linked at elbow or hand-in-hand in a chain across the front of the bodies initially, later opening to classical port de bras positions.
observation.hips_and_torso: Hips squared and stable, torso upright with slight upper back epaulement and head turns.
observation.partnering: None; dancers dance in unison holding hands with each other.
observation.levels_jumps_turns: Low jumps on pointe, traveling steps, ending in a low lunge/kneeling position on the floor.
observation.costume_and_props: Practice wear: leotards, tights, shorts, and pointe shoes; no hand-held props.
observation.cannot_infer: Exact foot articulation in rapid pointe work is partially occluded by distance and camera angle.

signature_moments.what: Four dancers linked hand-in-hand executing rapid side-to-side steps and small jumps on pointe in unison.
Repeating synchronized leg extensions and jumps while maintaining the linked arm chain.
Simultaneous descent into a low lunge/kneeling pose facing forward.
